39 What is a correct estimate of the order of magnitude of the diameter of a typical atomic nucleus?
A
10–14
m
B
10–18
m
C
10–22
m
D
10–26
m

hints: Notice the question asks for the diameter of the nucleus in $\text{m}$, not the diameter of the whole atom.
Recall that a typical atom is about $10^{-10} \text{ m}$ across and the nucleus is roughly $10,000$ to $100,000$ times smaller.
Check which power of ten gives a size a little larger than a single proton of about $10^{-15} \text{ m}$.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: order of magnitude only, so the nearest power of ten for nuclear diameter in $\text{m}$ is enough.
Recall the atomic scale: a typical atomic diameter is of order $10^{-10} \text{ m}$.
Recall the nuclear model from alpha scattering: the nucleus occupies only a tiny fraction of the atom, smaller by a factor of about $10^4$ to $10^5$.
Divide scales: $10^{-10} \text{ m} / 10^4 = 10^{-14} \text{ m}$, so the nucleus must be of order $10^{-15} \text{ m}$ to $10^{-14} \text{ m}$.
This is consistent with measured nucleon sizes, since a proton radius is about $10^{-15} \text{ m}$ and a larger nucleus contains many nucleons.
Therefore the estimate $10^{-14} \text{ m}$ fits, and the much smaller values would be below a single proton. This is option A.

A.explanation: Correct. A typical nucleus has diameter of order $10^{-15} \text{ m}$ to $10^{-14} \text{ m}$, about ten thousand times smaller than the atom.

B.explanation: Too small by about four orders of magnitude. $10^{-18} \text{ m}$ is smaller than a proton or neutron.

C.explanation: Far too small. $10^{-22} \text{ m}$ is much smaller than any known hadron or nuclear structure.

D.explanation: Far too small. $10^{-26} \text{ m}$ is far below the scale of quarks and nuclear forces.
